extracted.intended_audience: employers, small businesses, HR professionals, labor/employment attorneys, policy analysts, and other stakeholders interested in DOL FLSA EAP exemption rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble and regulatory analysis for the Department of Labor's final rule revising the EAP (white-collar) exemption salary and HCE compensation levels, including projection methodology, FRFA analysis, and updating mechanism. Provides assumptions, data sources, and cost/transfer estimation methods used to evaluate rule impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: EAP exemption tests
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify for the EAP exemption under the Department's regulations, the employee generally must meet three criteria: (1) the employee must be paid a predetermined and fixed salary that is not subject to reduction because of variations in the quality or quantity of work performed (the salary basis test); (2) the amount of salary paid must meet a minimum specified amount (the salary level test); and (3) the employee's job duties must primarily involve executive, administrative, or professional duties as defined by the regulations (the duties test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also includes the highly compensated employee (HCE) test with a higher salary threshold and a minimal duties test (2004 revision). Duties will continue to determine exemption status for most salaried white-collar employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salary level determination (standard salary level)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department is setting the standard salary level equal to the 35th percentile of weekly earnings of full-time salaried workers in the lowest-wage Census Region (currently the South), based on the most recent year (2023) of CPS data; using BLS 2023 data this equals $1,128 per week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To maintain effectiveness, the Department is finalizing an updating mechanism to update earnings thresholds on July 1, 2024 and every 3 years thereafter, with an exception for pausing future updates under certain conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: HCE compensation level
rubrics_metrics.description: The HCE total annual compensation requirement is adjusted to the annualized weekly earnings for the 85th percentile of full-time salaried workers nationally ($151,164 using 2023 data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chosen to ensure the HCE continues to serve its intended function of excluding all but those employees at the very top of the economic ladder, while not being as high as the original 2004 HCE percentile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of salary level as delimiting requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount paid to an employee is 'a valuable and easily applied index to the “bona fide” character of the employment' and is the 'principal[]' 'delimiting requirement' preventing abuse of the exemption; the salary level test saves time by narrowing who must undergo duties analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The salary level must be set so it restores overtime protections for those historically nonexempt (above long-test equivalence) while remaining below the short-test equivalence so employers can still use the exemption for many lower-paid white-collar employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (FRFA) required elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Regulatory Flexibility Act, when issuing regulations with significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, the agency must prepare a FRFA that (1) provides an overview of the objectives and need for the rule; (2) estimates the number of affected small entities and employees; (3) discusses reporting, recordkeeping, and other compliance requirements; (4) presents steps taken to minimize significant economic impact on small entities; and (5) declares awareness of any relevant Federal rules that may duplicate, overlap, or conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department treats this rulemaking as economically significant and includes the FRFA section to meet these statutory requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection methodology (six-step process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Projected costs and affected workers were estimated via: 1) use past growth in the earnings distribution to estimate future salary and compensation levels; 2) predict workers' earnings absent a change; 3) compare predicted earnings to predicted salary/compensation levels to estimate affected workers; 4) project future employment levels; 5) estimate employer adjustments to hours and pay; 6) calculate costs and transfers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These steps were applied in the 10-year projections and inform the numbers shown for affected workers, costs, and transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of affected EAP workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Affected EAP workers are those who would be exempt absent the rule change (e.g., would earn at least $684 if exempt under the standard salary level) but have projected earnings in the future year that are less than the relevant salary level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes workers who were not exempt in the base year but would become exempt absent the rule in subsequent years; affected status persists across years if projections keep them below the salary level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wage growth calculation (geometric growth rate)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department calculates future workers' earnings by applying the historical wage growth rate in the worker's industry-occupation, computed as the geometric growth rate in median wages using CPS MORG data for 2011-2023.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric growth rate is the constant annual growth rate that, when compounded, yields the last historical year's wage. OEWS 2012-2022 growth rates are used where CPS MORG has insufficient observations; remaining combinations use the median of CPS MORG growth rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment growth projection method
rubrics_metrics.description: Employment growth was estimated as the geometric annual growth rate based on the 10-year employment projection from BLS' National Employment Matrix (NEM) for 2022 to 2032 within an occupation-industry category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These growth rates are applied to sample weights to represent increased employment because the CPS MORG sample cannot be augmented with new observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer adjustments assumptions and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Employer adjustments to hours/pay are estimated in the first year the worker is affected and then applied to all future years in which the worker continues to be affected (unless the worker switches to a Type 4 worker). For newly affected workers in Years 2–10, the hours adjustment uses a long-run elasticity of labor demand of −0.4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workers' earnings in predicted years are earnings post employer adjustments, with overtime pay, and ongoing wage growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of direct employer costs (three categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department quantified three types of direct employer costs in the 10-year projections: (1) regulatory familiarization costs; (2) adjustment costs; and (3) managerial costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory familiarization costs occur in update years; adjustment costs are a function of newly affected workers (largest in Year 1); managerial costs recur each year for affected workers whose hours are adjusted and vary with update cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory familiarization cost assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory familiarization costs are assumed to be 10 minutes per establishment to access and read the published notice in the Federal Register with the updated standard salary level and HCE compensation level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This average was increased from 5 minutes in the 2016 rule; familiarization costs are incurred in Year 1 and update years (Years 4, 7, 10). Projected familiarization costs per update year are between $68.9 and $73.1 million.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment cost assumptions (per-employee time)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department estimates businesses will require an average of 75 minutes per employee to choose how to make adjustments for affected employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects that many affected workers will require little consideration (e.g., the ~70% who do not work overtime), and 75 minutes is an average incorporating more complex cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managerial cost assumptions (weekly time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Managerial costs are estimated at an average of 10 minutes per week per newly exempt worker who works overtime, reflecting time spent monitoring or enforcing policies to control overtime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department notes that nearly 70 percent of affected employees do not work overtime, and another 17 percent average about an hour of overtime per week, so average managerial burdens are expected to be modest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfers calculation components and dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department projects transfers from employers to employees due to the minimum wage provision and the overtime pay provision; transfers due to the minimum wage provision decline over time while transfers due to overtime pay grow slightly as the number of affected workers increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example projections: minimum wage transfers decline from $87.5 million in Year 1 to $22.6 million in Year 10; overtime transfers increase from $1.4 billion in Year 1 to $2.5 billion in Year 10 (using 2023$).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discount rate for average annualized costs and transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Average annualized costs and transfers are calculated using a 7 percent real discount rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: average annualized costs are $802.9 million and transfers $1.5 billion using the 7 percent real discount rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratcheting / conversion-to-hourly empirical standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical analyses of prior federal (2004) and California salary level increases did not find statistically significant increases in the percent of full-time white-collar workers paid on an hourly basis; thus the Department finds no evidence that periodic salary level increases cause widespread employer conversion of salaried workers to hourly status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department critiques commenters' and outside studies' assumptions that large shares of affected workers will lose salaried status and explains its own conservative modeling (e.g., assuming conversion of Type 2 and Type 3 workers only) yielding much smaller ratcheting estimates (approx. 2.5% upward effect by 2026 in a 2016-style analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Worker type classification for conversion analysis (Type 1–4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For modeling conversion-to-hourly the Department classifies workers as: Type 1—do not work overtime (majority of affected); Type 2—occasionally work overtime; Type 3—regularly work overtime and become nonexempt; Type 4—salaries increased to the new standard salary level and remain exempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department used these categories to bound the potential magnitude of conversion and to estimate a realistic upper bound by assuming all Type 2 and Type 3 workers convert to hourly (an assumption the Department believes overestimates real-world conversion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data source hierarchy and handling sparse data
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary wage data source is CPS MORG (pooled 2011-2023); where CPS MORG has insufficient observations, the Department uses geometric growth rates from BLS OEWS (2012-2022); any remaining occupation-industry combinations without sufficient data in either source are assigned the median of the CPS MORG growth rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This hierarchy ensures growth rates are available for all occupation-industry categories in projections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision not to replicate 2019 post-rule analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department did not replicate the analysis of the 2019 salary level increase because comparing quarters before and after the 2019 effective date would be confounded by the economic effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, making it impossible to isolate the impact of the 2019 rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should avoid before/after comparisons that coincide with major economic shocks that confound causal inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small entity impact assessment considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing impacts on small entities, the Department considered: whether enterprises meet FLSA enterprise coverage (excluding revenue from charitable activities), anecdotal reports from small firms, and standard thresholds (e.g., one to three percent of revenue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department included workers employed by enterprises that do not meet enterprise coverage requirements in estimates due to data limitations, and it concluded that even if all employees at a small entity were affected, payroll impacts would be about one percent of payroll per affected small entity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration (but non-quantification) of non-financial impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential non-quantified impacts include effects on worker flexibility, worker morale, loss of benefits, and career advancement; the Department acknowledges such impacts but did not quantify them due to lack of data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See referenced sections V.B.4.v and VII.C.3.v for discussion; employers can continue to offer flexible schedules and require monitoring under timekeeping rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions about employer responses (behavioral expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department assumes many employers facing large potential payroll increases will adopt alternatives such as limiting overtime hours rather than raising salaries to the new threshold; many employers already have timekeeping systems and policies that can be applied to newly nonexempt workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These behavioral assumptions underpin adjustment cost and managerial cost estimates and influence the projected distribution of costs versus transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification for routine updates to earnings thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department asserts that routine updates to part 541 earnings thresholds will ensure they keep pace with changes in employee pay and remain effective in identifying bona fide EAP employees; long intervals have eroded thresholds and created uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule includes a triennial updating mechanism with an option to pause updates under specified conditions to provide certainty and stability to employers and employees.
